Dhaaga Looms: Which Number Goes on the First Slide?

Mumbai, September 2026. A B2B textile marketplace has nine days to tell its board which single number it will be managed by for the coming year — and the number that got it funded is no longer the number that will keep it alive.

1. Nine days

At 9.40 p.m. on Monday, 7 September 2026, Sneha Iyer was the last person on the fourth floor of Dhaaga Looms' office in Lower Parel, Mumbai, holding a printout she had already marked up twice. The board meeting was on Wednesday, 16 September — nine days away — and the chief executive, Harsh Vora, had asked her for something narrower than a product update. He wanted one slide with one number on it: the number by which Dhaaga Looms would be managed for FY27, the number that would appear first in every monthly review, and the number against which the roadmap would be cut.

Sneha had been head of product for fourteen months. In that time the company's gross merchandise value had gone from ₹21 crore to ₹58 crore annualised, and GMV was the number on the first slide of every deck Dhaaga Looms had ever shown an investor. Harsh's instruction, delivered in a corridor, had been characteristically blunt: "Bring me the number you actually believe. If it is GMV, say so and I will defend it. If it is not GMV, you need to explain to Rajat why his bonus plan is wrong."

2. Company background

Dhaaga Looms was founded in 2021 as a business-to-business marketplace for fabric. On the supply side it aggregated 1,180 sellers: powerloom units in Bhiwandi and Surat, knitwear mills in Tiruppur, handloom weaver co-operatives around Varanasi and Chanderi, and a growing set of specialist dyers in Erode. On the demand side it served 2,340 buyers — small and mid-sized apparel brands, boutique labels selling on Myntra and Nykaa Fashion, uniform contractors, and a thickening layer of export houses shipping to West Asia and Europe.

The problem Dhaaga Looms had originally set out to solve was mundane and real. A boutique brand in Jaipur wanting 400 metres of a specific viscose blend had no reliable way to discover which of a hundred Surat units could supply it at what price, no way to verify quality before paying an advance, and no way to finance the sixty-day gap between paying the mill and being paid by Myntra. Dhaaga Looms answered the first two with catalogued, lab-tested swatches and an escrow-backed order flow on UPI and RTGS, and the third with a partner-financed credit line. It took a blended commission of 6.1 per cent, plus a logistics margin, and issued GST-compliant invoices that buyers could claim input credit against — a detail that mattered more to buyer adoption than anything the design team had ever shipped.

The market around it was crowded and getting more so. Reliance Retail and the larger Surat trading houses ran their own sourcing desks. Meesho and Flipkart's wholesale arms competed for the same small-brand buyers with deeper pockets. ONDC had, over 2025 and 2026, made catalogue interoperability cheap enough that Dhaaga Looms' original moat — knowing which mill could make what — was thinning. Against that, no competitor had yet matched its quality-inspection layer, which was slow, expensive and the single most cited reason buyers gave for returning.

3. The situation

Three things had happened over the previous four months, and Sneha's difficulty was that each pointed at a different number.

The first was that GMV had kept growing while the quality of that growth had deteriorated. In June, Dhaaga Looms had won a single Dubai-based modest-wear brand, Layaan Apparel, which placed orders of ₹40 to ₹60 lakh at a time against a negotiated commission of 2.2 per cent. Layaan was, by September, 17 per cent of GMV and 6 per cent of net revenue. Rajat Khanna, the sales head in New Jersey, had two more accounts of that shape in his pipeline and a bonus plan tied to GMV.

The second was that Anjali Deshpande, the data scientist in Toronto, had rebuilt the buyer-cohort tables in July and found that repeat purchase within sixty days had been sliding: 31 per cent for buyers acquired in the September 2025 quarter, 24 per cent for those acquired in the June 2026 quarter. Buyers were placing a first order, receiving fabric that was acceptable but not identical to the swatch, and quietly going back to their old Surat agent.

The third was that Shalini Nair, the customer-success lead in Singapore, had been arguing since May that the real constraint was neither growth nor repeat rate but the inspection layer. Her team handled 41 disputes in August, of which 29 were swatch-to-delivery colour variance. Each dispute consumed, on average, eleven working hours across two time zones and settled at an average credit of ₹34,000.

Lena Brandt, the designer in Berlin, had put the tension in a sentence during a video call that Sneha had written down verbatim: "Every screen I design is asked to do two contradictory things — help a new buyer place a first order in under ten minutes, and help a returning buyer re-order exactly what worked last time. We have been building the first one for two years because that is what the GMV number rewards."

4. The people

Harsh Vora, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai. Raising a Series B in the first quarter of 2027 and aware that the market rewards a legible growth curve. He wants one number, genuinely; he also knows which number makes the raise easier. He has told Sneha he will defend whatever she brings, and she believes him about eighty per cent.

Rajat Khanna, sales head, New Jersey. Hired for his export-house relationships and paid a quarterly bonus on GMV. He argues that large low-commission accounts are the fastest route to the ₹100 crore run-rate the Series B needs, and that margin can be repriced once volume exists. He is not wrong about the leverage; he is also the person with the most to lose from a metric change.

Anjali Deshpande, data scientist, Toronto. Sceptical of all aggregate numbers and the author of the cohort analysis in Exhibit 2. She wants the OMTM to be a cohort ratio and has said, in writing, that GMV at Dhaaga Looms' stage is "a measure of Rajat's calendar, not of our product."

Shalini Nair, customer-success lead, Singapore. Closest to the buyers who leave. She wants the company to be measured on something that captures fabric arriving as promised, because that is the only variable her team's day-to-day work touches. She is wary of a repeat-rate metric that her team cannot directly move.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 contains the case's central awkwardness in two adjacent columns. GMV rose 96 per cent across the five quarters, from ₹7.4 crore to ₹14.5 crore, which is the curve on Dhaaga Looms' first slide. Exhibit 2 is the number Anjali wants on the slide, and the last two columns explain why she wants it. 6. The options

Option A — keep GMV, and say why. Dhaaga Looms remains managed on GMV for FY27, with a target of ₹100 crore annualised by March 2027. The upside is coherence: the sales incentive, the investor narrative and the metric all point the same way, and large export accounts are genuinely the fastest route to a number that looks like scale. The cost is that the metric is provably insensitive to mix, that Exhibit 1 shows net revenue already flat, and that Dhaaga Looms would enter its Series B diligence with two years of declining commission and a repeat rate falling four quarters in a row — facts a competent investor will find.

Option B — switch to 60-day repeat order rate. The OMTM becomes the share of new buyers in a cohort who place a second order within sixty days, owned by Sneha, reviewed fortnightly with the acquisition-channel cut always shown, and used to decide whether the FY27 roadmap funds re-ordering and quality consistency or new-buyer acquisition. The upside is that it speaks to the risk the company has not closed and, per Exhibit 2, carries an 8.5-fold GMV multiple behind it. The costs are real: it matures eight weeks late, it can be improved by acquiring fewer buyers, it makes Rajat's bonus plan incoherent, and it is a smaller, less impressive-sounding number to put in front of a board.

Option C — switch to net revenue per active buyer. The OMTM becomes net revenue divided by active buyers, which fell from ₹7,656 to ₹6,698 across the five quarters in Exhibit 1. The upside is that it is money, immediately available, sensitive to both mix and repeat behaviour, and impossible to game with low-commission volume. The cost is that it is a blunt instrument for a product team: it moves for pricing reasons, mix reasons and product reasons at once, and Lena and Shalini would both struggle to name work that changes it in a quarter. It also tempts the company towards repricing Layaan before it has earned the right to.

7. Questions for discussion

1. State in one sentence the thing Dhaaga Looms has not yet proved about itself. Which of the three candidate metrics speaks to that sentence, and which speak to risks the company has already closed?

2. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3 present the same data. Why does GMV mislead here, and what would have to be added to GMV — rather than replacing it — for it to stop misleading?

3. Option B's metric can be improved by acquiring fewer buyers. What guardrails, with numeric thresholds and a named owner, would you attach to prevent that, and would they be enough?

4. Sneha has nine days. Which metric should she put on the slide, what should she say to Rajat about his bonus plan, and what condition should she write down now for when this metric must itself be retired?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an application of the idea that one metric matters at a time, and that the metric is chosen from the stage rather than from the strategy deck. The move the case asks for is not "pick the best metric" but "name the dominant unresolved risk, then pick the metric that speaks to it, then write down when it expires." GMV was the correct metric for Dhaaga Looms in 2023, when the open question was whether fabric buyers would transact online at all. That question was answered by 2025. From Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 the risk that now dominates is not whether buyers will transact but whether they will come back — and a metric blind to mix cannot see that risk at all.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It distinguishes the metric that sets the agenda from the metrics that constrain it, so that abandoning GMV as the objective does not mean stopping the reporting of GMV. It names an owner, a cadence and a specific decision the number will drive, because a metric attached to no decision is reporting dressed as management. And it states, in advance, the condition under which the chosen metric will be replaced — which is the part almost every team skips and the part that would have saved Dhaaga Looms two quarters of flat revenue.

One defensible path: Sneha adopts Option B as the FY27 OMTM, with three modifications. First, the metric is defined tightly — a second order of at least ₹50,000, placed within sixty days, excluding orders against dispute credits — and the acquisition-channel cut is mandatory at every review, so that the improvement cannot come from quietly narrowing the funnel. Second, two guardrails are written with thresholds and owners: new buyers acquired per quarter must not fall below 400 (owner: Rajat), and blended commission must not fall below 5.5 per cent (owner: Harsh). That second guardrail does the work Option C would have done, without making a blunt financial ratio the product team's objective. Third, the retirement trigger is stated on the same slide: when the 60-day repeat rate exceeds 35 per cent for two consecutive cohorts, the OMTM moves to net revenue per active buyer — at which point Rajat's large-account strategy becomes the right strategy rather than the wrong one, and his bonus plan can be rewritten to match.

The reasoning is that Dhaaga Looms' constraint is retention, that the ₹2.7 crore identified in Exhibit 2 from a single cohort is larger than anything the Layaan-shaped pipeline contributes to net revenue, and that a metric which matures in eight weeks is fast enough for a company with a fortnightly review and no immediate cash crisis. The path is defensible, not obviously right: a reader who believes the Series B is genuinely at risk without a ₹100 crore headline can argue Option A with a straight face, provided they also argue for the mix guardrail. What is not defensible is keeping GMV on the slide without ever having noticed that Exhibit 3's two lines had separated.

One Metric That Matters

What is the single number this stage lives or dies by — and how will you know when it is time to swap it for another?

1. A board meeting in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March, Ananya Deshmukh, VP of Product at Sopan Money, opened the board deck at slide four and felt the room lean forward for the wrong reason. Sopan Money was an eight-month-old, Series A-funded app that rounded up a user's UPI and card spends to the nearest ten rupees and auto-invested the difference into a liquid mutual fund. Slide four showed 240,000 downloads since launch, a number the board had watched climb every month and liked watching. Slide five, which Ananya had added herself, showed something the board had not been shown before: of those 240,000 downloads, only 96,000 people had even started the KYC flow, only 38,000 had ever completed a single auto-invest, and of that activated group, only 61 percent were still auto-investing four weeks later.

The immediate question on the table was blunt. Sopan Money's board wanted to approve ₹1.2 crore for a performance-marketing push — Instagram and YouTube creators, a cricket-season campaign — aimed at pushing downloads past a million by Diwali. Ananya's job that morning was to say which number the company should be steering by before it spent that money: downloads, activations, or the 61 percent retention figure that nobody on the board had asked about yet. Get this wrong and Sopan Money would spend a year's runway acquiring users who behaved exactly like the 61 percent who already quit — loudly visible, quietly gone.

2. The idea, stated plainly

The One Metric That Matters, usually written OMTM, is the single number a team agrees to treat as its primary compass for the specific stage its product is in right now, to the deliberate exclusion of every other number on the dashboard. The term comes from Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz's 2013 book Lean Analytics, written to solve a problem the authors had watched destroy early-stage teams repeatedly: a founder or product manager staring at twenty tiles on an analytics dashboard, each moving in a different direction, with no way to tell which movement should change what anyone does on Monday morning. Croll and Yoskovitz's answer was not "track fewer things" — teams still need many numbers for diagnosis. Their answer was to insist that at any given moment, exactly one of those numbers gets to be the one that determines whether this week counts as a win, and that this number changes as the business moves through recognisable stages of maturity.

The sentence Ananya could say in that boardroom without sounding glib was this: "We have not earned the right to optimise growth until we have proven retention, so for the next quarter, the one number that decides whether we are winning is week-four retention of activated users, not downloads." That sentence does two things a raw metric cannot do on its own: it names a decision the number will settle, and it implicitly names every other number — including the one the board most enjoyed watching — as secondary for now.

3. How the choice actually gets made

Picking an OMTM is not "pick your favourite KPI." It is a small sequence of decisions that most teams skip past too quickly, which is why the metric so often ends up being whatever number is already easiest to pull from the dashboard.

First, name the stage. Croll and Yoskovitz describe five recognisable stages a product typically passes through: Empathy (do people have the problem we think they have), Stickiness (do the people who try it keep using it), Virality (does usage spread on its own), Revenue (will people pay, and at what cost to acquire them), and Scale (can this grow into new segments or markets without breaking). Each stage answers one dominant question and treats every other question as background noise for now. Second, translate the stage's question into a single measurable number, phrased as a rate wherever possible rather than a raw count, because a rate tells you about the health of the system and a count mostly tells you about the size of your marketing budget. Third, set a line in the sand: a specific target value, and a date by which the team expects to cross it, because "improve retention" is not a metric, it is a wish. Fourth, assign an owner, a review cadence, and — the step teams skip most often — the actual decision the number will trigger once it crosses the line. If no decision changes when the number moves, it was never the OMTM; it was decoration. Fifth, and hardest, agree in advance on what will make the team retire this metric and pick the next one, so that "we hit our number" has a real endpoint rather than becoming a permanent scoreboard nobody revisits.

The staircase below is the mental model Ananya used to explain this to her own board: each stage sits on its own step, with its own dominant question and its own OMTM, and a team is only meant to be standing on one step's number at a time.

4. Sopan Money's arithmetic, worked in full

Ananya's team, led from Pune by growth analyst Kabir Mehta, had four candidate numbers on the table: total downloads (240,000), KYC starts (96,000), activated users who completed at least one auto-invest (38,000), and the 38,000's week-four retention rate (61 percent, meaning 23,180 users). She rejected downloads immediately: it measures the app store's opinion of the ad creative, not the product. She rejected raw activated-user count next, for a subtler reason — a count keeps climbing even while the underlying product is leaking users, because it never gets divided by anything.

That left a choice between the activation rate (38,000 ÷ 96,000 = 39.6 percent of people who start KYC ever complete a first auto-invest) and the week-four retention rate (61 percent of activated users still auto-investing a month later). She picked retention, on the reasoning that Sopan Money already knew people who try the product like it enough to finish KYC and invest once; what nobody yet knew was whether the product's core loop — small, automatic, monthly investing — was sticky enough to justify buying more of the same funnel. Spending ₹1.2 crore to widen a funnel with a leak at the bottom would only produce a bigger, faster leak.

The second column is not a forecast; it is a diagnostic. It shows Kabir's team what happens if the product squad fixes the KYC form — the actual bottleneck they had already flagged, where users abandoned mid-flow when asked to re-enter PAN details the app already had — while the downstream conversion rates (39.6 percent and 61 percent) stay exactly where they are. Even a 15-point jump in KYC completion, with nothing else improved, adds roughly 8,700 retained investors, more than a paid campaign was projected to add at the funnel's current, leaking conversion rates. This is the argument an OMTM is supposed to let you make with arithmetic instead of conviction: fix the step the current metric says is broken, and only then buy more traffic into it.

5. Seven distinctions a learner has to earn

OMTM is not your only metric. Sopan Money still watched a dozen numbers daily — server latency, fraud flags, app-store rating. OMTM names which one number changes a decision this quarter; the rest remain instruments on the dashboard, checked for problems, not chased for wins.

OMTM is not the North Star metric. A North Star, such as "monthly active invested rupees," is meant to hold roughly steady across a company's life as the number that best captures value delivered. OMTM sits underneath it and rotates every stage or two; confusing the two leads teams to either change their North Star too often or refuse to ever change their OMTM.

A rate is not the same claim as a count. 38,000 activated users and 39.6 percent activation rate can both be true and point in opposite directions if downloads are also rising; a growing count with a falling rate usually means the top of the funnel is being filled with worse-fit users.

Moving the metric is not the same as moving the business. The number can be improved through means that do not touch the underlying question it was chosen to answer — retention can be nudged upward temporarily with a cash-back push during exactly the measurement window, which is Goodhart's Law in miniature: a measure, once made a target, stops being a reliable measure.

Cohorts, not calendar snapshots. "Week-four retention" only means something when it is asked of a specific cohort of users who activated in the same window, tracked forward; a single day's snapshot of "percent of all users active this week" blends cohorts of wildly different ages and hides exactly the decay curve the metric exists to reveal.

A leading indicator is not a lagging one. Activation rate moves within days of a product change and lets a team react quickly; revenue moves months later and mostly confirms decisions already made. Teams under pressure to show quarterly progress are tempted to promote a lagging number to OMTM status because it sounds more serious, then discover it arrives too late to steer anything.

The number cannot tell you why. Sopan Money's 61 percent retention told Ananya there was a problem; it took five recorded user calls, run by a researcher in Hyderabad, to learn that most churned users had simply run out of round-up spend headroom on a single linked card. No OMTM, however well chosen, substitutes for finding out what the number is a symptom of.

6. The same idea, different products

The stage framework travels well, but what counts as the metric at each stage looks different depending on what kind of product it is, and how large the company already is.

SettingStickiness-stage OMTM tends to look like
Consumer app (Sopan Money)A per-user behavioural rate: week-four retention of activated users, cohort-based.
B2B SaaSA per-account, often per-seat, usage depth measure — e.g., share of licensed seats that logged a core action in the last 14 days — because one champion's enthusiasm can mask an unused deployment.
MarketplaceA liquidity ratio on the thinner side: for Sopan Money's later peer-lending pilot, the share of listed loan requests that found a matching lender within 48 hours, since both sides must be present for value to exist at all.
Early-stage team (under ~50,000 users)Small enough that the team can read individual user sessions; the OMTM is often paired with direct qualitative follow-up on every case that breaks the pattern.
Large, multi-product companyEach product line runs its own OMTM simultaneously; the discipline shifts from choosing one number to preventing twelve teams' twelve numbers from silently overriding one another's priorities.

The common thread is that the metric always tries to capture the one behaviour that proves the current stage's core assumption, scaled to whatever unit — a user, an account, a two-sided match — actually carries that assumption in that kind of business.

7. Where teams get this wrong

Disagreement reveals there is no real OMTM yet.

8. What good looked like, six months later

By September, Sopan Money had spent nothing on paid growth. Instead, the product team had rebuilt the KYC flow to pre-fill PAN and address from the linked bank account, and had shipped a setting that let a user add a second card once round-up headroom on the first ran low — directly answering what the Hyderabad interviews had surfaced. Week-four retention of activated users had moved from 61 to 74 percent, against the 65 percent line Ananya had set in March, and the team retired that OMTM on schedule rather than continuing to celebrate a number that had already done its job. The next number up, chosen deliberately and announced in the same September board deck, was the share of retained users who had also referred at least one contact who completed KYC — the Virality-stage question, asked only once Stickiness had actually been earned, not assumed.

9. What Ananya decided, and two questions to sit with

Ananya told the board to hold the ₹1.2 crore campaign for one quarter, set week-four retention at 65 percent as the line that would unlock it, named Kabir as owner with a fortnightly review, and specified in advance that the metric would be retired the moment it crossed the line, replaced by whatever number best captured the next stage's question. The board approved the delay unanimously once the funnel arithmetic showed what a leaking bottom would have done to the campaign's return. What she had actually decided was smaller and more durable than any one number: that the team would always be able to say, out loud, which single figure decided this week's verdict, what decision crossing its line would trigger, and when it would stop being that figure. The natural next idea to study is the North Star metric that OMTM nests beneath, since the two are easy to confuse and each misused makes the other harder to use well. Before moving there, sit with two questions: what decision at your own workplace would actually change if this week's number moved, and can you name, right now, the condition under which your current headline metric will be retired?

One Metric That Matters

The discipline is not choosing a number. It is choosing which single uncertainty a team is allowed to be curious about this quarter — and building the arithmetic that says when that permission expires.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 4 February 2026, in a converted textile shed in Pune's Bhosari industrial belt, Rukmini Bhide, VP of Product at Ferozi Devices, watched her CEO put up a slide she had asked him not to. Ferozi sold connected reverse-osmosis water purifiers on subscription: no upfront purchase, ₹549 a month, filters and servicing included, a cellular module reporting flow rate and membrane pressure back to Pune. The slide read Installed base: 148,000 units, up 71% YoY. It was true, and it was the number Ferozi had steered by for three years. Rukmini had spent January building the case that it was now the most dangerous number in the company.

Her arithmetic, which nobody had disputed and nobody had acted on, was that the average unit installed in 2025 would lose Ferozi money over its life, and that every additional install made the loss larger. The board wanted to hear about a Series C anchored to installed base. Rukmini wanted 2026 spent steering by a number almost nobody outside the service organisation had heard of, and installed-base growth slowed to a third of its rate while it happened.

Eight days later, in Hyderabad's Financial District, Meghna Iyer faced a structurally identical argument with none of the same evidence available to her. Meghna was Chief Product Officer at Chhandas Systems, which sold claims-adjudication workflow software to general insurers — thirty-four accounts, average contract value ₹62 lakh, sales cycles of nine to fourteen months. Chhandas had steered for two years by signed logos, and its board had the same affection for that number that Ferozi's had for installs. Meghna wanted to replace it with depth of use: the share of licensed adjudicators at each account completing at least one claim end-to-end in a given week, currently 41 percent.

Her head of customer success, Aditya Rane in Mumbai, agreed with the diagnosis and objected to the metric. With thirty-four accounts, he argued, the number would wobble by more than it moved: two large accounts going live would swing it six points, and the team would spend a year reading weather as climate. He was not wrong. What makes the Chhandas case the more instructive of the two is that the right metric was obvious and, at that company's size, very nearly unmeasurable.

2. The idea, precisely stated, and the argument about it

The One Metric That Matters is a commitment device. Formally: for a bounded period a team nominates one quantity as the sole arbiter of whether its work is succeeding, defines the threshold at which the nomination ends, and demotes every other quantity to diagnosis. Three clauses do the work. Sole arbiter means it settles disputes, not that it is the only thing measured. Bounded period means it is scheduled to die. Demoted to diagnosis means other numbers may veto — a guardrail breach stops a launch — but may not authorise: a rising secondary number cannot declare a quarter successful.

Alistair Croll and Benjamin Yoskovitz named the idea in Lean Analytics (2013), but the move is older and draws on two traditions still in tension. One is the operations-research tradition of the single objective function: you cannot optimise two things at once, so if you will not choose, the optimiser chooses for you, usually badly. The other runs through management by objectives to Amazon's distinction between output metrics and controllable input metrics — the observation that attention is a company's scarcest resource, and that a metric's job is less to describe the world than to ration attention.

The problem it was invented against is not innumeracy. Croll and Yoskovitz were writing about teams with too much data: twenty dashboard tiles, each defensible, moving in different directions, from which any Monday-morning decision could be justified after the fact. OMTM is a restraint on post-hoc rationalisation, and its value lies in what you give up.

Four schools disagree about how far to take that, and it is worth stating what each will and will not sign.

SchoolWill signWill not sign
Singularity (Lean Analytics lineage)One number arbitrates; the rest are diagnostic; the number rotates by stage.That a balanced set can substitute. They read every scorecard as an invitation to pick the flattering row afterwards.
Metric tree / input metrics (Amazon lineage; much of modern growth practice)One stable output metric with three to five owned, controllable inputs, each carrying a causal claim.That one number can be controllable, fast-moving and meaningful at once. Rukmini and Meghna, without using these words, stood in different schools. Rukmini's case was unit-economic: she had the cash arithmetic and wanted permission to follow it. Meghna's was closer to the input-metric school by necessity, because her candidate number failed a measurement test.

3. Mechanics: what experts actually do, and the arithmetic under it

Practitioners describe choosing an OMTM as a judgement call. Watched closely, the good ones do something mechanical: they write the objective as an equation, differentiate it, and ask which terms they can both move and see.

Step one: write the objective, not the metric

Ferozi's objective, once Rukmini's analyst Tanmay Ghoshal in Kolkata wrote it out, was lifetime contribution per unit:

L = (P − s) × T − H

where P is the monthly subscription (₹549), s monthly service and consumable cost (₹186 blended), T expected tenure in months (19.4 for the 2024 cohort) and H amortised hardware and installation cost (₹7,400). That gives L = 363 × 19.4 − 7,400 = ₹655: positive, barely. For the 2025 cohort, tenure 18.1 months and service cost ₹198, L = 351 × 18.1 − 7,400 = −₹1,048. Ferozi was paying ₹1,048 for each new install it celebrated.

Step two: differentiate, to find where a point of movement is worth most

The partial derivatives are elementary and almost never written down. At 2025 values: one extra month of tenure is worth ₹351; one rupee off monthly service cost, ₹18.10; one rupee on price, ₹18.10 before demand response; one rupee off hardware, exactly one rupee. Stated that way, the company's instinct — negotiate harder with the membrane supplier — was worth a fraction of a tenure gain per unit of effort.

The second-order effect is where the real answer was, because tenure and service cost are not independent. Tanmay's survival analysis showed that units with two or more unscheduled visits in their first twelve months churned at 3.1 times the rate of units with none, and that only 46 percent of the 2025 cohort reached month twelve with zero visits. One quantity was driving both terms at once. That is the structural property experts look for and beginners miss: the best OMTM candidate is usually not a term in the objective function but a common cause behind two of them.

Step three: test whether you can see the movement you need

This is the step most often skipped, and it decided the Chhandas case. A metric is decision-grade only if plausible movement exceeds noise at the cadence you review it. Chhandas had 1,180 licensed adjudicator seats across 34 accounts. Naively, a proportion on n = 1,180 has a standard error near 1.4 percentage points and everything is detectable. But seats are clustered inside accounts, and adjudicators at one insurer behave alike. Priya Nambiar, the analytics lead in Kochi, estimated the intra-class correlation at ρ = 0.22 with a mean cluster size of 35. The design effect is 1 + (35 − 1) × 0.22 = 8.48, so the effective sample is 1,180 / 8.48 = 139 seats and the true standard error nearer 4.2 points. To call a quarterly change real, Chhandas needed roughly 2.8 standard errors of the difference — about 11 points. Realistic quarterly movement was three to four.

Step four: name the retirement trigger before you start

An OMTM without a stated death condition becomes a permanent scoreboard. Mature teams write three: a threshold, crossed and held for two review periods; an exhaustion condition, where a marginal fortnight of dedicated work moves it less than some stated amount; and a falsification condition, where the question it was chosen to answer gets answered no and the right response is to change the product, not the metric. Ferozi wrote all three in February.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

The doctrine holds only under conditions. Stated as testable claims, and applied to both protagonists:

Where the idea is actively misleading is worth being blunt about. First, when two uncertainties are genuinely co-equal — the cold start of a two-sided market, where each side makes the other worthless in its absence — forcing one number produces a company excellent at half a market. Second, during a regime change, when historical relationships between metric and objective break and the metric keeps reporting confidently in a language that no longer applies. Third, in defensive situations, where the job is to not lose rather than to learn and a portfolio of guardrails genuinely beats a single objective. Fourth, before product–market fit, when no quantity is stable enough to aggregate and forty customer conversations teach more than any rate.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product. When Chhandas added a fraud-triage module, the clean answer — one OMTM per line — broke at the seam: the same 34 accounts and the same customer-success team served both, so the two numbers competed for the same finite hours of customer change management. Mature companies do not solve this by choosing; they make the contention explicit and force a quarterly allocation argument in which the shared resource is the currency. What they say they run is a metric tree. What they actually hold is a meeting where two directors argue over one customer-success manager's calendar.

Two-sided. Ekatra Bazaar, a Coimbatore marketplace connecting restaurants to vegetable and staples wholesalers, spent a year arguing whether its OMTM was buyer retention or seller fill rate. The resolution is to pick the constraint, not a side: one side binds at any moment, and the OMTM belongs there until it moves. Ekatra's constraint was supply reliability, so fill rate won — but the team wrote that if fill rate passed 90 percent without buyer repeat following, the constraint had moved and the metric must move with it.

Regulated. Chhandas's customers answer to IRDAI, and claims turnaround time is a regulated disclosure — a metric they cannot ignore and Chhandas cannot own. The expert move is to separate the metric that arbitrates internally from the one the regulator and the customer's auditor already watch, and to ensure the internal number leads the external one rather than competing with it.

Hardware plus software. Ferozi's is the general case: hardware puts a large, irreversible, front-loaded cost into the objective function, so payback is long and the OMTM must be a cohort property read over months. Software teams used to weekly readouts find this intolerable and reach for a faster proxy. Sometimes that is right. Often it produces a company optimising install velocity because install velocity is the only thing that feels like progress.

AI-native. Ekaagra AI, a Bengaluru company selling a legal-research assistant to mid-sized firms, met the sharpest version of the Goodhart problem. Its OMTM was queries per active lawyer per week, which rose 40 percent in a quarter while renewal intent fell: a less reliable model produced more re-querying, so usage rose because quality had fallen. Ekaagra moved to the share of research tasks where the generated memo was exported and cited without substantive edit. In a product where the system does the work, interaction volume and value delivered can move in opposite directions, so the metric needs an acceptance clause built in.

6. Nine distinctions that separate command from competence

The metric is a causal claim, not a description. Nominating the zero-visit share says Ferozi believes service incidents cause churn, not merely that the two correlate. The tell is that an expert can state the counterfactual their metric assumes and how they would learn it was false. The obvious reading — a metric as neutral summary — is wrong, because neutral summaries cannot be falsified and what cannot be falsified cannot be retired on evidence.

Common causes beat objective terms. Beginners pick a term from the equation because it is visible in the P&L. Experts look one layer beneath for the quantity driving two terms at once, where leverage is multiplicative rather than additive. The tell is that an expert's metric sounds operational rather than financial — service visits, not gross margin — while still being defended in rupees.

Measurement design is part of the choice. Meghna's metric was right and unusable until the unit of analysis changed. Competent practitioners treat detectability as the analyst's problem, arriving after the choice; experts treat it as a constraint on the choice, and will sometimes prefer a slightly less relevant metric that can actually be read. The tell is a PM who asks, before adopting a number, what its standard error is at the intended cadence.

The rate is not always better than the count. The received wisdom that rates beat counts is right about vanity metrics and wrong about capacity-constrained businesses. Ferozi's service organisation needs an absolute visit count, because technicians are fixed headcount and a falling rate against a growing base still overwhelms them. Experts ask what the number is being used to size, and choose ratio or magnitude accordingly.

A metric with no losing side has not been adopted. If demoting a number costs no one anything, nothing was demoted. At Ferozi the losing side was the service organisation, paid on visits closed; at Chhandas it was sales, paid on logos. The tell of a real change is that a compensation or hiring plan moves within a quarter. Where the metric changes and nothing else does, the old metric is still quietly running the company.

Cohorts age; calendars do not. A hardware business with growing installs has a base whose average age falls as it grows, so a blended churn rate can improve simply because the base is younger — the company looks healthiest exactly when it is installing most and losing most. Experts separate mix effects from behaviour effects, and the tell is that they ask what the base's average tenure did before interpreting any change in an average.

Proxy relationships decay, and decay is measurable. The correlation between a proxy and the objective it stands for should itself be tracked. Where it falls, the proxy has decoupled — usually through something that games the measurement, sometimes through an honest change in the business. The obvious reading, that a metric either is or is not a good proxy, is wrong: proxies are good for a while, and knowing how long is most of the skill.

The review cadence is part of the metric. A number reviewed weekly that carries signal only quarterly gets over-interpreted fifty-two times a year, and teams thrash; a fast-moving number reviewed quarterly wastes its principal virtue. Experts state cadence and metric together as one object, and treat a request to review more often as a request to change the metric.

The best teams keep a shadow scorecard and admit it. No serious company truly watches one number; finance never stops watching cash, legal never stops watching exposure. The mature practice is a one-page guardrail sheet with explicit breach thresholds, published beside the OMTM. The failure is pretending it does not exist, because then guardrails get consulted only in a crisis, when they read as accusations rather than instruments.

7. How it differs by product type and stage — and where it does not

SettingWhat genuinely changes
ConsumerHigh n makes detectability a non-issue; Goodhart risk binds instead, since consumer metrics are cheap to game with incentives and notifications.
B2B and enterpriseLow n makes detectability the binding constraint; metrics shift to repeated observation of the same units and cadence lengthens. Buying centre and using centre differ, so usage and renewal can diverge for a year.
Platform and marketplaceThe metric sits on the currently binding side. What changes is not the technique but the duty to state in advance what evidence would show the constraint has crossed.
Hardware and physical goodsFront-loaded irreversible cost lengthens the horizon; monthly cohorts replace weekly readouts; capacity constraints legitimise counts alongside rates.
AI productsUsage and value can move in opposite directions, so the metric needs an acceptance clause. Variable inference cost brings unit economics in earlier than in conventional software.
Pre-PMFArguably does not apply; qualitative evidence dominates and aggregates are unstable.
Growth stageClassic case. One number, fast cadence, clear retirement trigger.
Scale and multi-productThe technique survives, but the hard part moves from choosing a number to arbitrating between teams' numbers competing for shared resources.

Two things do not differ, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than manufacturing distinctions. That the metric must name a decision it will settle is invariant across every setting above, as is the requirement of a written retirement condition. Everything else — unit, cadence, tolerance for counts, number of guardrails — is contingent.

8. Three worked examples

Ekatra Bazaar: the metric that worked

Ekatra's fill rate — orders delivered complete within the promised four-hour window, as a share of orders accepted — stood at 62 percent in April 2025 across 2,900 monthly buyers; twelve months later, 88 percent. Orders per active buyer per month rose from 5.4 to 9.1 and buyer 90-day retention from 44 to 67 percent. The instructive part is the arithmetic that justified the choice in advance: at 62 percent fill, a buyer ordering weekly met a failure every 2.6 weeks, which interviews suggested was the threshold beyond which restaurants kept a parallel wholesaler alive; at 88 percent the interval became 8.3 weeks. The metric was chosen because someone had computed where the behavioural cliff sat.

Devrai Naturals: the metric that was right and too slow

Devrai, an Indore direct-to-consumer skincare brand, chose 90-day repeat purchase rate as its OMTM in 2024. It was the correct metric for the question, and also — with a 90-day lag plus the time to accumulate a readable cohort — a number that told the team in October what its July decisions had done. Devrai kept it and added a written leading indicator, the share of first orders containing a second product, which predicted 90-day repeat with a correlation of 0.61 and was readable in a fortnight. An OMTM whose feedback loop is longer than the team's decision cycle needs a nominated fast companion, with the correlation stated as a number and re-estimated quarterly.

Aviral Power: the metric that failed, and the recovery

Aviral Power, a Chennai operator of public EV charging points, adopted sessions per charger per day as its OMTM in early 2024, at 4.2. Over six quarters it rose to 6.8, a 62 percent improvement the company reported enthusiastically. Contribution per charger per month fell over the same period from ₹9,400 to ₹6,100.

Sessions per charger is a site-level average, and the fastest way to raise it is to add chargers where demand is already dense, which nudges each site's numerator while adding capital and rent the average never sees. Aviral was rewarding itself for redistributing demand it already had.

The recovery took two quarters and was not a metric change alone. Aviral moved to contribution per charger-month against a site-level payback threshold of 31 months, wrote off 40 chargers in three over-served Chennai corridors, relocated 26 to highway sites on the Bengaluru and Tirupati routes where utilisation was lower but dwell time and tariff were higher, and changed the site-acquisition team's target from chargers commissioned to sites clearing payback. Twelve months on, sessions per charger had fallen to 5.9 while contribution per charger per month recovered to ₹11,200. The durable lesson was procedural: Aviral now re-estimates the correlation between its OMTM and contribution every quarter and treats a fall below 0.4 as an automatic review trigger.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late

Every early warning in that table is a comparison, not a level. No single reading reveals any of these failures; each needs the number set beside something else — its own history, its standard error, the objective it stands for, the age of the base. Teams that review only the current value are structurally blind to all six.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether one number is safe at all. The singularity school holds that attention is the binding constraint and any set larger than one gets chosen after the fact; its evidence is that teams with balanced scorecards report success every quarter. The guardrail school holds that Goodhart effects are so reliable at scale that a lone metric is a gaming instrument with a fuse on it, and points to Aviral. For the first to be wrong, Goodhart effects would have to arrive faster than metrics can be rotated; for the second, divided attention would have to cost more than gaming — plausible in small teams, implausible in large ones. Both are probably right at different sizes, which is not a synthesis; neither school accepts that framing.

Whether the metric should be controllable or meaningful. The input-metric school insists a team's number must be something it can move by Friday, or ownership is fictional. The outcome school insists a controllable input is exactly what is easiest to game, and that teams should carry a number they only partly control so they are forced to influence what they do not own. Chhandas sits on this fault line: Meghna's metric depends on an insurer's own change management, and reasonable colleagues disagreed about whether that made it the right metric or an unfair one.

Whether it applies before product–market fit. One camp argues the earliest stage is where focus matters most. The other argues pre-fit aggregates are unstable, n is tiny, and a number there substitutes a false sense of progress for the conversations that would teach something. The evidence is mixed and anecdotal, which is itself informative: nobody has a clean dataset on companies that died, and survivorship makes the question close to unanswerable today.

Whether a financial metric may ever be the OMTM. The unit-economics school says that once a product is sold rather than discovered, cash arithmetic outranks behaviour. The behavioural school says financial outcomes lag too far to steer by and aggregate too many causes to diagnose. Ferozi's resolution — a behavioural metric chosen by explicit financial differentiation — is one way through, available only to a company whose objective function can be written down. Many cannot.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a candidate metric. Someone who has internalised it arrives with an objective function, a derivative, a standard error and a date. They ask what decision the number will settle before asking whether it is a good number. They write the retirement condition in the adoption document and diarise it. They know the standard error at their review cadence and refuse, out loud and in front of the board, to interpret moves smaller than it. They track the proxy's correlation with the objective as a metric in its own right. They can name who lost something when the metric changed, and if nobody did, they treat the adoption as incomplete. And when a new number is proposed, their first question is not whether it matters but whether anything they would do differently depends on it — which dissolves most proposals in a minute.

12. What Rukmini and Meghna decided

Rukmini won on 26 February, though not in the form she proposed. Ferozi adopted the zero-visit twelve-month cohort share, targeting 70 percent by March 2027, reviewed monthly, owned by Tanmay. Two things made it real. The service organisation's incentive moved from visits closed to units reaching twelve months without a visit, which cost an uncomfortable conversation with a long-serving regional head in Nagpur. And the board accepted a written growth ceiling: installs capped at 6,000 a month until the cohort share passed 60 percent, since each install beyond that was a ₹1,048 liability. The retirement trigger was written down: threshold held two quarters, or a fortnight of work moving the number less than half a point.

Meghna's decision was less dramatic and arguably harder. She adopted seat-week activation over a rolling twelve-week window, reviewed monthly, with the standard error printed on the slide every time the number appeared. She did not change the sales compensation plan, judging that she could not carry both fights at once, and wrote in the adoption memo that this was the single most likely reason the metric would fail. She scheduled a review for July. Whether she was right to defer it is still arguable.

  1. Ferozi capped installs to protect a unit-economics repair. Had the zero-visit share reached 70 percent but installed-base growth never recovered, would the decision have been wrong — and what evidence available in February would have shown it?
  2. Meghna printed a standard error on a board slide. What does that cost a product leader politically, and when is the cost worth paying?
  3. Aviral's correlation with contribution fell from 0.71 to 0.18 in data the company already held. What organisational arrangement, rather than what analysis, would have made someone look?

13. Going deeper

North Star metric
The stable outer number an OMTM temporarily serves; right nesting prevents both a North Star that changes yearly and an OMTM that never does.
What makes a good metric
The property checklist a candidate must pass before the leverage and detectability arithmetic is worth doing at all.
Vanity vs actionable metrics
The sharpest filter for the failure Ferozi suffered for fourteen months, and the vocabulary for arguing it without insulting the person holding the number.
GAME framework
A structured route from goal to metric that catches the skipped step: naming the decision before the number.
Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions
The three families an OMTM sits within; the family tells you which levers are even available this quarter.
Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio
The formal treatment of two choices handled operationally here: proxy decay, and when a count legitimately beats a rate.
Attention, transaction, productivity games
A typology of what a product competes for, which constrains the shape of a sensible OMTM before any arithmetic.

Dwaar Secure: The Number on the Board Slide

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 11 October 2026. Nine months of cash, a term sheet that expires in six weeks, two businesses wearing one company's name, and six numbers that cannot all be true at once.

1. Sunday night

At twenty past eleven on Sunday 11 October 2026, Kabir Sheth was sitting on the floor of his flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with eleven printed pages fanned out in front of him and his laptop open on the sofa behind him. The board met at ten the next morning in Mumbai; he would join from Bengaluru on video, which meant that unlike Meenal he would not be able to read the room before he spoke.

The slide he had been asked to bring was slide four. Meenal Joshi, Dwaar Secure's co-founder and chief executive, had been explicit in her Friday note: "Slide 4 is the number we are managed by for FY28. One number, Kabir. Ravi will ask what we would do differently at half that number and at double it, and he will ask what we stopped doing because of it. Bring the answer, not the options." Ravi Bhargava chaired Dwaar Secure's board on behalf of its Series B lead, and had a reputation for asking the second question twice.

Kabir had four candidate numbers written on the top sheet in blue ink, and a fifth crossed out. Beside them, in pencil, he had written a sentence he had not shown to anyone: "I am not sure we are one company." At 11.40 p.m. a message arrived from Tanvi Raikar in Toronto, where it was early afternoon: "Re-ran the cohort pull. Telemetry and app numbers still don't reconcile. Down to 31 pp gap, not 37. Do you want the reconciliation slide or not?" He did not reply immediately.

2. Company history, and one decision that still binds

Dwaar Secure was founded in Pune in 2021 by Meenal Joshi, formerly a product manager at a large appliance maker, and Devansh Patel, a mechanical engineer who had spent nine years designing lock mechanisms. Their thesis was that Indian gated communities — the 200-to-900-flat towers going up across Hinjewadi, Whitefield, Gachibowli and Noida Extension — were being secured by a register at the gate and a lock designed in the 1970s, and that a camera-equipped smart lock priced under ₹12,000 could change that.

The first product, Dwaar One, shipped in late 2022: a battery-powered deadbolt with a fingerprint reader, a PIN pad, a 1080p camera in the escutcheon, and a companion app. It competed, then and now, with Godrej's Advantis range, Yale's India line-up, Qubo from the Hero group, and a long tail of imported units sold on Amazon and Flipkart. Distribution came through Croma and Reliance Digital shelves, Amazon.in, an installer network of 340 electricians, and — increasingly — builders who specified Dwaar at project handover.

The decision that still bound the company was taken in August 2024. To win a 3,100-unit specification with Zahran Developments, a Dubai-based developer with towers in Dubai Marina and two projects in Bengaluru, Dwaar Secure agreed to bundle what the contract called Lifetime Cloud into the hardware price: unlimited event-video storage, visitor logs and family sharing, for the life of the device, with no renewal event and no separate line item. Zahran's procurement head had been unmovable on the point; Yusuf Kadri had closed it in nine days; the order was worth ₹27 crore of hardware over two years and it put Dwaar Secure into an export market. Meenal had signed.

By October 2026, 61 per cent of Dwaar Secure's installed base sat on Lifetime Cloud plans — the Zahran units, plus every builder specification signed after them, because builders had learned to ask for the same terms. Those households generated no recurring revenue, would produce no renewal decision until at least FY28, and, as Ramya Kulkarni the chief financial officer had pointed out in June, cost the company roughly ₹41 a month each in storage, egress and support.

The second constraining decision was smaller and more recent. In March 2025, to defend the ₹7,999 price point against imported units, Devansh shipped Dwaar Lite: no camera, no cloud, local fingerprint only, no app requirement. Dwaar Lite was 34 per cent of units shipped in the September 2026 quarter and was, by design, incapable of appearing in any engagement or subscription metric.

3. The industry

The Indian smart-lock market in 2026 was growing fast and consolidating slowly. Godrej and Yale held the trust of builders and the older buyer; Qubo had moved aggressively on price and bundled it with its camera range; Reliance Retail and Croma had begun to favour whichever brand funded the shelf; and Amazon's Great Indian Festival in September routinely compressed a quarter of retail demand into eleven days, at a discount the brand funded. Dwaar Secure's differentiation, insofar as it had one, was the app: family sharing, delivery-partner PINs generated for Swiggy Instamart and Zepto drops, a maid-attendance log that the Singapore team reported was the single most-mentioned feature in renewal conversations, and integration with the visitor-management systems used by resident welfare associations.

Three external forces bore directly on the board's question. The first was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose consent and purpose-limitation requirements Dwaar Secure had implemented in January 2026. Camera-derived features — face-based unlock, visitor snapshots, the maid-attendance log — now required explicit, revocable, per-purpose consent. Roughly 29 per cent of households on Dwaar One had declined at least one consent, which meant they used the lock but generated a much thinner event stream, and made the company's own engagement analytics a partial view of reality by law rather than by accident.

The second was GST and channel economics. A ₹11,999 lock sold through Croma yielded Dwaar Secure roughly ₹7,100 after trade margin, taxes and installation subsidy; the same unit sold direct on its own site yielded ₹9,400 but at a customer-acquisition cost that Nikhil Raghavan's team put somewhere between ₹1,100 and ₹2,800 depending on who was asked.

The third was export exposure. The Zahran relationship had opened a UAE pipeline worth, on Yusuf's forecast, ₹40 crore over FY28, all of it at Lifetime Cloud terms and all of it requiring data residency arrangements that Farhan Qureshi's team had costed at ₹1.4 crore of one-time work plus ₹18 lakh a quarter.

4. The situation in detail

Dwaar Secure had been managed, since November 2022, on a single number: cumulative units activated. The metric had been chosen when the open question was whether Indian households would fit a camera-bearing lock to their front door at all, and it had served well through 2023 and 2024. It crossed 100,000 in February 2026 and stood at 168,400 at the end of September 2026. Meenal used it in every investor conversation. It appeared on the company's careers page.

The trouble began in April 2026, when Grace Lim's customer-success team in Singapore — which handled the UAE and Singapore accounts as well as India's escalations — reported that 22 of the 31 Zahran towers had stopped raising tickets entirely. Grace's read was that this was bad news, not good: a building with 180 locks and no tickets in four months was probably a building where people had stopped using the app. Farhan disagreed, and pulled firmware telemetry showing 81 per cent of Zahran devices had sent a heartbeat in the previous thirty days.

In June, Tanvi Raikar in Toronto was asked to reconcile the two views, and could not. The app analytics pipeline showed a thirty-day active rate of 44 per cent across the camera-equipped base; firmware telemetry showed 78 per cent. The gap was 34 points. Tanvi's memo listed six candidate explanations, of which four were plausible and none could be eliminated with the instrumentation the company had: the analytics software development kit had shipped only in Android app v4.2 and later; iOS event forwarding had been broken between February and June; a heartbeat was emitted by any mains-connected unit whether or not a human touched it; and households that had declined DPDP consents produced no app events for several of the flows the pipeline counted.

In July, the Series C process began, and with it a change in the questions. Dwaar Secure's prospective lead asked, in its first diligence list, for monthly recurring revenue, net revenue retention and subscription attach rate. The answers were, respectively, ₹1.94 crore, a number the company could not compute, and 23 per cent. 8. The options as Kabir currently sees them

Option 1: keep cumulative units activated. Nothing changes before the Series C closes on 22 November. The metric is understood by every function, it is auditable, Devansh's organisation stays aligned to it, and Meenal's slide three and slide four tell one story. Kabir's own note against this option reads: "we will be managed for another year by a number that went up in every quarter that Exhibit 5 went down."

Option 2: switch to monthly engaged households. Defined as a household with at least one app-verified use of a core feature in thirty days, measured on the camera-equipped base. This is Grace's position and partly Tanvi's. It speaks to the question of whether anyone is getting value. It also has a 34-point measurement band, excludes 34 per cent of new units by construction, is depressed by a legal consent regime the company cannot change, and would be reported to the board with a footnote longer than the number.

Option 3: switch to contribution margin per household per month. Ramya's position, and the one that connects to the runway. It is sensitive to mix, to Lifetime bundling and to serving cost, and it would immediately make the Sharjah deal visibly expensive. Its weaknesses are that it is an allocation rather than a measurement — Exhibit 5's footnote puts the September figure anywhere between ₹16 and minus ₹4 depending on one assumption — and that no product manager in the company could name three things to ship next quarter that would move it.

Option 4: switch to day-90 device reporting. Farhan's position: the share of units still reporting ninety days after activation. It is available for every unit including Lite, it is fast, it is hard to game from the software side, and it would make installation quality the company's headline concern. It would also make the company's number a measure of the device rather than of the household, and Kabir has written beside it: "measures that we did not break, not that they got anything."

Underneath the four options, in the margin of the top sheet, Kabir has written the sentence he has not shared. Dwaar Secure sells a ₹7,999 mechanical lock through Croma to a household that will never open an app, and a ₹27 crore ten-year cloud commitment to a Dubai developer, and a ₹147-a-month remote-monitoring service to an engineer in New Jersey. The four options all assume the answer is one number for all of it. He does not know whether the board will hear that as insight or as evasion, and he has forty minutes of the agenda.
